<reason>PRO built a clean cost-benefit structure (opt-in, self-limiting cost; near-elimination of the dominant risk profile on every matched ride; supply recruitment) and then narrowed the debate to a decidable question: does partial coverage disqualify a safety feature? CON's case rested almost entirely on the 11 p.m. suburban scenario and an "enough" standard that effectively required the feature to work when supply is thinnest. PRO's reframe in A4.3/A5.3—that rides and incidents cluster where matching is thick, so the "easy hour" is where most harm actually occurs—undercut CON's central weighing, and CON's only reply was to call it a "luxury filter billed as night safety," which quietly substitutes CON's own framing for the motion. CON's "crude proxy" point was neutralized by A2.5 and never rehabilitated. CON did land real hits: gender preference is not a niche SKU like wheelchair vans, identity/fraud ops are nontrivial, and PRO conceded leftover inventory is the inefficiency. But CON never sized those costs, and its attempt to name a rider whose risk rises (B4.1) was largely status-quo outcomes relabeled, as A5.1 exposed. PRO's two clipped turns are an execution cost but the lost material was concluding text. Clear but competitive win for PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question A3.1 ("name one rider whose risk goes up") forced CON into B4.1, whose examples (a woman who walks or hails an unvetted car after seeing no match; a non-opting rider whose male-driver share rises from nearly-all to nearly-all) PRO dismantled in A5.1 as "the status quo described suspiciously," leaving PRO's arithmetic—some rides safer, none less safe—essentially intact.</best_rebuttal>
